claims.text: Cu can segregate to the surface of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Surface segregation produces an elemental concentration gradient from the particle surface to its core.
Surface enrichment with Cu lowers the local cohesive energy at the particle surface.
The lower local cohesive energy reduces the energy barrier for surface melting.
Cu-enriched surface regions act as nucleation sites for premelting.
Premelting initiated at a segregated surface propagates inward through the nanoparticle.
Enhanced surface segregation causes an earlier premelting onset than occurs in a homogeneous nanoparticle.
Enhanced surface segregation causes a more pronounced surface-melting feature than occurs in a homogeneous nanoparticle.
Five-element nanoparticles can exhibit homogeneous elemental mixing without significant segregation or phase separation.
Rapid quenching produces Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles with minimal surface segregation.
A tailored thermal pretreatment can be used to enhance surface segregation relative to a rapid-quenched baseline.
Cu has a comparatively small cohesive contribution because of its fully occupied d-band, making metallic bonds involving Cu less energetically favorable.
Cu surface segregation can lower a high-entropy alloy's internal energy.
The premelting regime for these nanoparticles is approximately 0.75–1.05 times the bulk melting temperature.
A homogeneous nanoparticle without detectable surface segregation has a higher and more spatially uniform premelting onset temperature.
The proposed mechanism is limited to well-controlled, single-phase solid-solution high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles near 0.75–1.05 Tm.
Particle-size effects can dominate the premelting response and thereby limit the proposed segregation mechanism.

A lack of a statistically significant difference in premelting onset or melting progression between segregation-enhanced and homogeneous particles would falsify the proposed governing role of surface segregation.
